report.source_text: The CT scan, performed with contrast administration in a single portal-venous phase with positive oral contrast, revealed two saccular images adjacent to the greater curvature of the stomach, exhibiting peripheral calcifications and measuring up to 28 x 23 mm, the largest of the two. These lesions appeared to follow a vascular trajectory. However, the absence of dedicated simple or arterial phases made interpretation challenging. Notably, the enhancement pattern of the vascular lesions with intravenous contrast resembled that of the oral contrast observed within adjacent small bowel loops (Figure 1). High-density fluid was also observed in the pelvis (up to 86 Hounsfield Units -HU-), suggesting associated hemoperitoneum (Figure 2).

Angiography is needed to confirm the vascular nature of these lesions and identify if they are dilatations of the gastroepiploic artery causing the hemoperitoneum.

report.source_text: Selective abdominal arteriography was indicated with the diagnostic suspicion of visceral aneurysms as the cause of hemoperitoneum. Images of arteriography showed the usual vascular anatomy of the celiac trunk with its three main branches: splenic artery, left gastric artery, and common hepatic artery (Figure 3). The catheter was navigated to the gastroduodenal artery, where new acquisitions were made. At this time, three saccular dilatations were documented in the gastroepiploic artery, the largest of them in the left gastroepiploic artery, one more in the middle third, and the smallest in the right gastroepiploic artery (Figure 4A). Using a microcatheter, occlusion of the described aneurysms was performed by implanting coils. Arteriographic controls showed successful exclusion of the gastroepiploic artery, with preservation of other visceral branches of the celiac trunk (Figure 4B).

Arteriographic controls showed successful exclusion of the gastroepiploic artery, with preservation of other visceral branches of the celiac trunk (Figure 4B). After four days of hospital surveillance and ensuring clinical and laboratory stability, the patient was discharged without pain with recommendations and warning signs.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An 82-year-old patient presented with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain, pallor, sweating, orthostatism, and abdominal tenderness, along with signs of hypovolemic shock (pulse 108 bpm, BP 98/56 mmHg) and anemia (Hb 9.2 g/dL). A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast revealed high-density fluid in the pelvis (86 HU), consistent with hemoperitoneum, and two saccular images adjacent to the greater curvature of the stomach, following a vascular trajectory (E001). Subsequent selective abdominal arteriography documented three saccular dilatations in the gastroepiploic artery (left, middle, and right gastroepiploic artery) (E002). Occlusion of these aneurysms was performed by implanting coils, with arteriographic controls showing successful exclusion of the gastroepiploic artery (E002). The patient was discharged after four days of hospital surveillance, clinically and laboratory stable, and without pain (E003).
